617.title: The pull home
617.hook: Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, homesick for his bride
617.howItsDone: Nanda's story is often told in Buddhist communities, and in the Anguttara Nikaya Nanda is named foremost among monks in guarding the senses, the discipline he came to after his struggle.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the king and queen on the rooftop, and your line, everyone loves themselves. Did you spare someone a slight? Today, a monk who can't stop thinking about home. Day six hundred seventeen.

First semester away. The new place is supposed to be the start of everything, and the student lying awake can only think about the kitchen at home, the dog, someone's voice saying come back soon. Nanda had his own version of that. He was the Buddha's half-brother, the son of Mahapajapati, and he had become a monk. But one day he tells the other monks: I'm not happy living this life. I can't keep it up. I'm going to give up the training and go back. Why? Because of a girl. Today: the pull home.
screen: `FIRST SEMESTER AWAY.` → `NANDA, THE HALF-BROTHER.` → `I CAN'T KEEP IT UP.`

segments.voice: When I left home, Nanda tells the Buddha, a Sakyan girl, the loveliest in the land, looked up at me with her hair half combed and said: come back soon, master. I keep remembering it. What the Buddha does next is startling. He takes Nanda by the arm and, the text says, as easily as a strong man bends his arm, the two vanish and appear in the heaven of the Thirty-Three. There Nanda sees five hundred heavenly nymphs. Which is lovelier, the Buddha asks, the Sakyan girl or these? Next to these, Nanda says, she's nothing at all. Then practice, the Buddha says, and I promise you these. So Nanda practices. But the other monks hear about the deal and start teasing him: Nanda the hired hand, Nanda working for wages. Ashamed, Nanda goes off alone and practices in earnest. And somewhere in that practice, the wanting itself falls away, both the girl and the nymphs. He goes back to the Buddha and says: I release you from your promise. I already knew, the Buddha says. The verse praises one who has crossed the mud of sense-desire and is no longer shaken by pleasure or pain. Some readers take the story as a bigger desire used to loosen a smaller one, until both drop away. And the ending is plain in the text: the pull wasn't beaten by force. It simply stopped pulling.
screen: `COME BACK SOON, MASTER.` · `THE HEAVEN OF THE THIRTY-THREE.` · `NANDA THE HIRED HAND.` · `I RELEASE YOU FROM YOUR PROMISE.` · then, large: `THE PULL HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what pulls you back. Sit and settle. Ask, gently: what tugs at me when I try to keep a good intention? A habit, a person, a comfort, a picture in my head? Let it come, the way Nanda's memory came, the half-combed hair, the voice. Don't fight it and don't follow it. Just feel the pull in the body, where it lives. Then rest with the breath, and notice that the pull, too, rises and fades. The bell holds the time.
Nanda. The Buddha's half-brother, homesick for the girl he left, until the wanting itself fell away. Today's word.
Your line: it simply stopped pulling. Today, when an old habit tugs at you, name it, feel it, and watch how long it lasts if you don't follow it. Day six hundred seventeen.

what it means: one desire was used to loosen another, until in real practice both fell away and the promise was released.

618.title: Not yet ripe
618.hook: Meghiya insists on going alone and is overwhelmed; five things ripen the mind
618.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the Meghiya Sutta to explain why practice is done with a teacher and a community, and the five supports it lists are taught across Theravada monastic life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nanda and the girl with her hair half combed, and your line, it simply stopped pulling. Did you watch one tug rise and fade? Today, a monk who wants to go too fast. Day six hundred eighteen.

Meghiya is serving as the Buddha's attendant. One morning, coming back from alms in a village, he walks along a river and finds a mango grove so lovely he can hardly stand it. Quiet, shady, by the water. The perfect place to meditate, he thinks. He hurries back and asks permission to go and sit there. Wait, the Buddha says. We're alone here. Stay until another monk comes. Meghiya asks again. Wait. A third time. And this time the Buddha says: what can I say, when you speak of striving? Go, Meghiya. Today: not yet ripe.
screen: `A MANGO GROVE BY THE RIVER.` → `WAIT UNTIL ANOTHER COMES.` → `WHAT CAN I SAY? GO.`

segments.voice: Meghiya goes and sits under a mango tree in the perfect grove. And there, in the perfect place, his mind is overrun. Three kinds of thought keep coming at him: thoughts of sense-pleasure, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harming. He's amazed: I went forth out of faith, and here I am, swarmed by these. He comes back and tells the Buddha everything. The Buddha doesn't say I told you so. He says that when the mind's release is not yet ripe, five things bring it to ripeness. First, a good friend, a good companion. Second, keeping the training, living with integrity. Third, talk that actually helps: about wanting little, contentment, solitude, energy, wisdom. Fourth, effort, letting go of what's unskillful and taking up what's skillful. Fifth, wisdom that sees how things rise and pass. And notice which comes first. The good friend. The very thing Meghiya walked away from, when he left the Buddha alone to sit in his beautiful grove. Then the Buddha adds what to do with the thoughts: reflect on the body's unattractiveness to ease lust, kindness to ease ill will, mindfulness of breathing to cut the chatter, and seeing impermanence to uproot the conceit I am. The place wasn't the problem. Meghiya wasn't ready yet, and the Buddha could see it. Ripeness can't be rushed.
screen: `THE PERFECT PLACE, A RESTLESS MIND.` · `NO I TOLD YOU SO.` · `FIVE THINGS THAT RIPEN.` · `FIRST, THE GOOD FRIEND.` · then, large: `NOT YET RIPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one piece of advice. Sit and settle. Bring to mind one piece of advice you've been given lately and brushed aside: from a parent, a friend, a doctor, a teacher. Let yourself hear it again, without defending against it. Ask, is there something here I'm not ripe enough to see yet? You don't have to decide anything. Just let it be heard. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kalyanamitta, a good friend. Meghiya rushed to a perfect grove and was overwhelmed; the Buddha named five things that ripen the mind, starting with this. Today's word.
Your line: a good friend comes first. Today, when you want to skip ahead, ask whether the fruit is ready, and whether a friend might see something you don't. Day six hundred eighteen.

what a scholar hears: Udana 4.1 speaks of aparipakka cetovimutti, the 'unripe release of mind', and its five dhammas appear again as a set in AN 9.3.

619.title: Each held a part
619.hook: the blind men and the elephant, read whole
619.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the elephant story when teaching about clinging to views, and versions of it are also told in Jain, Hindu and Sufi traditions, each with its own lesson.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Meghiya in the mango grove, and your line, a good friend comes first. Did you let one piece of advice be heard? Today, a story from earlier this year, read again from its home in the Udana. Day six hundred nineteen.

Near the start of this year, on day three hundred fifty-eight, you heard the blind men and the elephant: water pot, winnowing basket, plowshare, broom. It turns up on posters and in classrooms, and other traditions tell it too. Short retellings often keep only the middle, and drop how it starts and how it ends. Today we're reading it whole, from its place in the sixth chapter of the Udana, and paying attention to three things the short version leaves out: who it was told to, the line about the king, and the verse. Today: each held a part.
screen: `WATER POT, BASKET, PLOWSHARE, BROOM.` → `SHORT VERSIONS KEEP THE MIDDLE.` → `TODAY, THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. The monks come back from town troubled. Teachers of many groups are arguing: is the world eternal or not, finite or not, is the soul the same as the body, does one who is awakened exist after death. And they're wounding each other, the text says, with mouths like daggers. So the story is told to the monks, about a city full of argument. Second, the king. After the blind men fight with their fists, the text says simply that the king was delighted. Why? The text doesn't explain. Some readers hear him as a man enjoying a spectacle he arranged; others hear the delight of someone who sees the whole while the others see parts. The text leaves it open, and so will we. And notice something easy to miss: none of the men lied. The one at the ear really did feel a winnowing basket. Each report was true about its part. What went wrong was the word only. Third, the verse, which the Buddha speaks after telling the story. Some teachers and seekers, it says, are attached to these views. They quarrel and dispute, people who see just one side. Look at the shape of it. The problem isn't seeing a part; everyone sees a part. The problem is clinging, and then fighting. Last time the lesson was hear out a view you dislike. Today it goes further: listen to the whole, before you judge.
screen: `MOUTHS LIKE DAGGERS.` · `THE KING WAS DELIGHTED.` · `NO ONE LIED; THE WORD WAS ONLY.` · `PEOPLE WHO SEE ONE SIDE.` · then, large: `EACH HELD A PART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen fully before judging. Sit and settle. Bring to mind a recent moment when you made up your mind about someone before they'd finished talking. Replay it slowly. What part were they holding? What part were you holding? Is there a word only hiding in your own view? Don't argue it out. Just let both parts sit side by side, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Ditthi, a view or opinion. In Udana 6.4, every blind man's report was true about his part; the quarrel came from clinging to one side. Today's word.
Your line: listen to the whole. Today, in one conversation, wait until the other person has completely finished before you decide anything. Day six hundred nineteen.

screen: `DAY 619 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOTHS AND THE LAMP.`

620.title: The moths and the lamp
620.hook: insects flying into the oil lamps at night
620.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the image of insects and a flame for craving that harms the one who craves, drawing on scenes like this one in the Udana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the elephant read whole, and your line, listen to the whole. Did you let someone finish before you decided? Today, a scene in the Udana that's over in a few lines. Day six hundred twenty.

A porch light on a summer night. Moths come out of the dark, circle the bulb, bump it, drift off, circle again. A bulb is one thing. An open flame is another: a moth that flies into a candle or an oil lamp doesn't come out again. Why do they keep coming? The Udana doesn't try to explain the moths. It just watches them. Today: the moths and the lamp.
screen: `A PORCH LIGHT ON A SUMMER NIGHT.` → `A FLAME IS DIFFERENT.` → `THE UDANA JUST WATCHES.`

segments.voice: The whole story takes a few lines. The Buddha is sitting outdoors in the dark of the night, and oil lamps are burning. Many winged insects are flying around them, and falling into the lamps, one after another, to their harm, to their ruin. The Buddha sees this. And, knowing the meaning of it, he speaks the verse. Rushing up, passing by what's essential, they bring on new bonds again and again, like insects falling into a lamp. So some are bound up in what is seen and heard. That's all. No crowd, no question, no long teaching. A man sitting in the dark, watching. And notice the word in the middle: passing by what's essential. The moths aren't stupid. They're drawn by something real, the light. The trouble is that they mistake the light for something it isn't, and they keep coming back. The verse says people can do the same with the seen and the heard, the bright thing on the screen, the voice that pulls us, rushing to it again and again, each time tying another knot. There's a link back to Bahiya, a few days ago: in the seen, only the seen. The moth doesn't stop at the seen. It flies straight in. And there's something quiet in the scene, too. The Buddha doesn't put out the lamps or explain the insects. He sits in the dark, sees them, and speaks about people.
screen: `OIL LAMPS BURNING IN THE DARK.` · `FALLING IN, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `PASSING BY WHAT'S ESSENTIAL.` · `BOUND BY THE SEEN AND THE HEARD.` · then, large: `THE MOTHS AND THE FLAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one flame you fly into. Sit and settle. Ask: what bright thing do I keep circling, even when it burns a little? A feed, a fight, a craving, a particular kind of evening that always ends the same way. Picture it as a lamp in the dark. Watch yourself circling it, with kindness, the way the Buddha watched the moths. You don't have to stop yet. Just see the circling. The bell holds the time.
Adhipataka, a moth. In the Udana, insects falling into oil lamps at night: the picture of rushing again and again to the seen and the heard. Today's word.
Your line: the moths and the flame. Today, when you feel the pull toward your bright thing, pause one breath before you fly in. Day six hundred twenty.

fork.reveal: the text says only that he saw, and spoke the verse. the scene is short, and it's about us as much as the moths.

621.title: She still gave
621.hook: Suppavasa, in a long and hard pregnancy, still gives; she is safely delivered
621.tomorrow: A hundred dear, a hundred sorrows
621.howItsDone: In some Theravada communities families invite monks for a meal and a blessing around a birth, and protective chants are sometimes recited for women in childbirth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: insects falling into the lamps, and your line, the moths and the flame. Did you pause one breath before flying in? Today, a woman in pain who still thinks of others. Day six hundred twenty-one.

A hospital waiting room. The coffee goes cold. The clock seems broken. Every time the door opens, every head looks up. The Udana tells of a woman named Suppavasa, a Koliyan noblewoman, whose wait the text measures in years. The text says she carried her child for seven years, and was in labor for seven days. Readers take those numbers in different ways; what's plain is a very long, very hard wait. And in the middle of it, she does something unexpected. Today: she still gave.
screen: `A HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM.` → `SUPPAVASA, THE KOLIYAN.` → `A VERY LONG, VERY HARD WAIT.`

segments.voice: In her pain, the text says, Suppavasa holds on to three thoughts. The Buddha teaches the way out of suffering like this. His community practices the way out of suffering like this. And there is a peace where suffering like this doesn't exist. The teacher, the community, the peace: held in labor. Then she sends her husband to the Buddha, to bow at his feet in her name and tell him how she is. The Buddha says: may Suppavasa be well and free from illness, and give birth to a healthy son. And at that moment, the text says, she does. Then the part the title is about. As soon as she's able, Suppavasa sends her husband back to invite the Buddha and the monks for meals, seven days in a row. She has just come through seven days of labor, and her first wish is to give. The Buddha even asks her: would you want another child like this one? And she says yes, she would have seven more. The verse that follows is surprising: what is unpleasant comes disguised as pleasant, the hateful as dear, pain in the form of happiness, and overwhelms the heedless. Readers take it in different ways; some hear it as the Buddha seeing her joy and her pain held together. Tradition says the child grew up to be the monk Sivali, remembered for how freely gifts came to him.
screen: `THREE THOUGHTS, HELD IN LABOR.` · `MAY SHE BE WELL.` · `SEVEN DAYS OF MEALS.` · `PAIN IN THE FORM OF HAPPINESS.` · then, large: `SHE STILL GAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless someone who is waiting. Sit and settle. Think of someone who is in a long wait right now: for a baby, a diagnosis, a visa, a job, a phone call. Picture them where they are. Then simply wish them well, the way the Buddha wished Suppavasa well, that she be well and free from illness. Let the wish be quiet and plain, in your own words or none. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers. The bell holds the time.
Dana, giving. Suppavasa, after a long and terrible labor, invited the Buddha and the monks for seven days of meals. Today's word.
Your line: give one small thing anyway. Today, on a hard day, offer a meal, a minute, or a kind word. Day six hundred twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 621 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A HUNDRED DEAR, A HUNDRED SORROWS.`

622.title: A hundred dear, a hundred sorrows
622.hook: Visakha grieves a grandchild; how many would you want to love?
622.howItsDone: Visakha is honored in Theravada tradition as a model lay disciple, and teachers sometimes tell her story alongside Kisa Gotami's when speaking about grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Suppavasa, and your line, give one small thing anyway. Did you give one small thing on a hard day? Today, another woman, another child, and a much harder morning. Day six hundred twenty-two.

Visakha is a lay follower the early texts honor for her generosity; tradition says she built a monastery in Savatthi. One day, the Udana says, a granddaughter she dearly loved dies. Visakha comes to the Buddha in the middle of the day, her clothes wet, her hair wet. The text doesn't say why; some readers take it as the washing after a funeral. Why have you come here, the Buddha asks, at midday, with your clothes and hair wet? She tells him. And he answers with a question. Today: a hundred dear.
screen: `VISAKHA, THE GIVER.` → `WET CLOTHES AT MIDDAY.` → `HE ANSWERS WITH A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Visakha, he asks, would you like to have as many children and grandchildren as there are people in Savatthi? Yes, she says. Of course. And how many people die in Savatthi each day? Ten, she says. Or nine, or five, or one. Savatthi is never without someone dying. Then, he says, if you had that many, would you ever be without wet clothes and wet hair? No, she says. Enough with so many. And then the Buddha says it plainly: those who have a hundred dear ones have a hundred sorrows. Those who have ninety have ninety. And so on, down to one: one dear, one sorrow. Those who have none dear have no sorrow. Then the verse. Grief and lamentation and all the many kinds of suffering in the world exist because of what is dear. Where there's nothing dear, they don't. You may remember Kisa Gotami from the first year, carrying her son from house to house. And not long ago, the dart of grief. This is the same teaching from another side. Notice how the Buddha does it. He doesn't tell Visakha her grief is a mistake. He lets her do the arithmetic herself. Buddhist teachers read the line in more than one way. Some say it's about clinging, holding the dear as mine, not about ceasing to love; the same canon praises boundless kindness to all. Others hear in it the monk's path of renunciation. What's clear is the math, and that she worked it out herself.
screen: `AS MANY AS LIVE IN SAVATTHI?` · `NEVER A DAY WITHOUT A DEATH.` · `ONE DEAR, ONE SORROW.` · `SHE DOES THE ARITHMETIC.` · then, large: `A HUNDRED DEAR, A HUNDRED SORROWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold dear ones with care. Sit and settle. Bring to mind one person you love. Feel how dear they are. Now notice, gently, whether an edge of fear comes with it: that they might be hurt, or leave, or die. If it does, that's the sorrow the Buddha was counting. Don't push the love away. Just loosen your grip a little, the way you'd hold a bird: close enough to keep it warm, open enough to let it breathe. The bell holds the time.
Soka, sorrow. The Buddha's words to the grieving Visakha: a hundred dear ones, a hundred sorrows; one dear, one sorrow. Today's word.
Your line: with an open hand. Today, tell one person they're dear to you, and hold that truth with an open hand. Day six hundred twenty-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: love always brings sorrow, so don't love.
what it means: each dear one carries a sorrow; Visakha sees it herself, and some teachers read it as a teaching about clinging.
what a scholar hears: Udana 8.8 (Visakha Sutta) belongs to the Pataligamiya chapter; a related teaching on sorrow born of the dear is MN 87, Piyajatika Sutta.

623.title: There is an unborn
623.hook: there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade; were there not, there'd be no escape
623.howItsDone: The saying on the unborn is studied in Theravada teaching on nibbana and is quoted by teachers of many Buddhist schools; it also appears in the Itivuttaka (Iti 43).

segments.voice: Yesterday: Visakha's wet hair at midday, and your line, with an open hand. Did you hold someone dear with an open hand? Today closes a week, with a short saying about what isn't made. Day six hundred twenty-three.

Everything you've ever touched was born, or made, or put together. Your phone. Your house. Your body. Your mood this morning. Every one of them came from causes, and every one of them will come apart. That's the whole teaching of impermanence, which you've heard many times on this path. And it raises a hard question. If everything is made, and everything comes apart, is there anything at all that isn't? Is there a way out of the making? In the eighth and last chapter of the Udana, the Buddha answers with four words that start with un. Today: there is an unborn.
screen: `EVERYTHING YOU'VE TOUCHED WAS MADE.` → `EVERYTHING MADE COMES APART.` → `IS THERE A WAY OUT?`

segments.voice: The setting is a talk on nibbana to the monks. And here's the saying, as close as we can come. There is, monks, an unborn, an unbecome, an unmade, an unconditioned. If there were not this unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, no escape would be known from the born, the become, the made, the conditioned. But because there is, an escape is known. Notice where the weight falls: on two small words, there is. Not it might be, not we hope. The text doesn't describe the unborn at all. It argues for it, from the escape: if there were only the made, there'd be no way out of it. The fact that the path leads somewhere shows there's somewhere to arrive. How do traditions read it? Theravada teachers generally read the unborn as nibbana itself, not a self, not a soul, not a creator, but the unconditioned. Other schools have drawn on the passage in their own ways. The text itself simply says, there is. Look back at the week. Nanda's pull home. Meghiya not yet ripe. The elephant read whole. Moths at the lamp. Suppavasa giving. Visakha's hundred sorrows. Every one of them was about the born and the made. Today, the Udana points past them.
